area: Area VII. Emergencies and Accident Reporting
objective: By the end of this lesson you can tell an aircraft accident from an incident using the 49 CFR 830 definitions, name the incidents that need an immediate call to the NTSB, and say how to notify, what to preserve and when the written report is due.
why: Most pilots never need 49 CFR 830, so they forget it, and then have to decide in a farm field with shaking hands. The rule turns on exact definitions: a broken wrist, a bent spar, an in-flight fire or a lost propeller tip each trigger a call, while a bent prop from a taxi strike does not. Accident reporting requirements of the NTSB are a required knowledge area for the private and commercial certificates.

prereading.what: The whole rule: definitions, immediate notification, what to say, preserving wreckage and records, and the written report.

warmup: Think first: you land a rented Cessna 172 on a soft grass strip. The nose wheel digs in, the propeller tips curl and the nose gear fork bends. Nobody is hurt and the fuselage looks fine. Is this an aircraft accident? Do you call the NTSB tonight, file a report within 10 days, or neither? Write down your answer and the reason, then check it at the end of chunk 3.

key_terms.def: An occurrence tied to operating an aircraft, between the time anyone boards with the intention of flight and the time all have got off, in which a person dies or is seriously injured, or the aircraft gets substantial damage.
Any injury that results in death within 30 days of the accident.
An injury that meets any one of five tests in 830.2: hospital stay over 48 hours, most bone fractures, severe bleeding or nerve, muscle or tendon damage, internal organ injury, or serious burns.
Damage or failure that hurts structural strength, performance or flight characteristics and would normally need major repair or replacement of the part. 830.2 lists common damage that does not count.
An occurrence other than an accident, tied to operating an aircraft, that affects or could affect safety of operations.
One of the incidents in 830.5(a) that needs immediate notification even if no one is hurt, such as an in-flight fire or a flight control failure.
Under 830.2, any person who causes or authorizes the operation of an aircraft, such as the owner, lessee or bailee. The operator must notify and report.
The call or message to the nearest NTSB office, made right away by the fastest means available, required by 830.5.
The written report form. Due within 10 days after an accident; for a listed incident only if the NTSB asks.
An aircraft that has not arrived when expected. Under 830.5(b) one believed to have been in an accident must be reported at once.
Aviation Safety Reporting System: voluntary safety reports sent to NASA. The FAA does not use them for enforcement, except information about accidents or crimes.
An incident in which a collision was possible because aircraft came within 500 ft of each other, or a pilot reports a collision hazard existed. Reported to the FAA, not under 830.

chunks.title: Who investigates, and why 830 is yours to know

body.p: The PHAK history says the newly created NTSB took over the role of the old Civil Aeronautics Board and was charged with investigating all transportation accidents in the United States [[1:21|PHAK 1-6]]. Today both the NTSB and the FAA investigate aviation accidents. The NTSB finds the probable cause and makes recommendations. The FAA looks for gaps in pilot training, aircraft certification, air traffic control and its other areas [[30:10|RMH 1-1]].

bullets: FSDO inspectors handle general aviation accident investigation at the request of, or in cooperation with, the NTSB [[24:26|AFH 1-5]].

49 CFR 830 covers notification and reporting of accidents and incidents of U.S. civil aircraft wherever they happen, and of foreign civil aircraft when the event happens in the United States, its territories or possessions [[60:880|49 CFR 830.1]].
Its wreckage preservation rules apply to civil aircraft accidents in the United States and its territories or possessions [[60:880|49 CFR 830.1]].
You must show your pilot certificate, medical certificate and logbook to an authorized NTSB representative on reasonable request [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)]].

callout.text: Accident reporting requirements of the NTSB are a required aeronautical knowledge area for the private pilot certificate [[60:295|14 CFR 61.105(b)(2)]] and for the commercial pilot certificate [[60:310|14 CFR 61.125(b)(2)]].

body.p: The end product of an NTSB investigation is a final report like this one. Note the fields at the top: aircraft damage and injuries. Those are exactly the two things the 830.2 accident definition is built on [[25:185|AIH 10-1]] [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

check.q: Which agency determines the probable cause of an aviation accident?
check.a: The NTSB. The FAA investigates too, but looks for deficiencies in its own areas such as training, certification and ATC [[30:10|RMH 1-1]].

chunks.title: What counts as an aircraft accident

callout.text: Aircraft accident: an occurrence associated with the operation of an aircraft, between the time any person boards with the intention of flight and the time all such persons have disembarked, in which any person suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

bullets: Three triggers, any one is enough: a death, a serious injury, or substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Fatal injury means an injury that results in death within 30 days of the accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
The time window starts when anyone boards with the intention of flight and ends when everyone has got off [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. A taxi mishap with people on board is inside the window.
The definition also takes in unmanned aircraft accidents, which have their own definition [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

head: Serious injury: any one of these
Source
rows: Hospitalization for more than 48 hours, starting within 7 days from the date of the injury
A fracture of any bone, except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose
Severe hemorrhages, or nerve, muscle or tendon damage
Any injury that involves an internal organ
Second or third degree burns, or any burns affecting more than 5 percent of the body surface

callout.text: Application: the tests are about the injury, not about how the person feels at the scene. A passenger who walks away with a sore wrist that later proves broken has a serious injury [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Ask injured people to tell you what the doctor finds.

body.p: Interpretation: because the window opens only when someone boards with the intention of flight [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]], damage done while pushing an empty airplane into a hangar falls outside the accident definition. The rule text says nothing more about such cases.

check.q: A passenger breaks a toe (a simple fracture) getting out after a firm landing. Nothing else is hurt or damaged. Accident?
check.a: No. Simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose are excluded from serious injury, and there is no death or substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

chunks.title: Substantial damage, and the damage that does not count

callout.text: Substantial damage: damage or failure that adversely affects the structural strength, performance or flight characteristics of the aircraft, and that would normally require major repair or replacement of the affected component [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

head: Not substantial damage by itself (830.2)
Source
rows: Engine failure, or damage limited to an engine, if only one engine fails or is damaged
Bent fairings or cowling; dented skin; small punctured holes in the skin or fabric
Ground damage to rotor or propeller blades
Damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes or wingtips

body.p: A major repair is one that, if done wrong, might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation or flight characteristics, or one not done by accepted practices or elementary operations [[60:10|14 CFR 1.1]]. Interpretation: so the two definitions line up. If fixing the damage would be a major repair to structure, the damage is likely substantial.

Damage like this, with the wing and fuselage structure crushed, plainly affects structural strength [[28:204|AWH 16-15]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]. Most cases are less clear, and the call depends on what a mechanic finds.

The AFH teaches you to use the wings, landing gear and fuselage bottom as dispensable structure that absorbs the stop and keeps the cabin intact [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. In a tree landing, both wings and the fuselage underside take the first contact [[24:355|AFH 18-6]]. Application: a well-flown emergency landing can still be an accident on paper. That is fine; the AFH is clear that sometimes the airplane should be sacrificed so the occupants walk away [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

Crops can stop an airplane with repairable damage [[24:351|AFH 18-2]], and a gear-up landing on soft level ground may cause less damage than gear down [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Interpretation: whether either is an accident depends on whether the damage goes past the excluded items (gear, flaps, ground damage to the propeller, dents) into structure [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

check.q: Warm-up answer: soft-field landing, propeller tips curled, nose gear fork bent, fuselage fine, nobody hurt. Accident?
check.a: Not by these facts. Ground damage to propeller blades and damage to landing gear are not substantial damage, and no one was hurt [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]. If the mechanic finds the firewall or engine mount structure damaged, look again.

chunks.title: Incidents: most are not reported to the NTSB

callout.text: Incident: an occurrence other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft, which affects or could affect the safety of operations [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

body.p: That definition is very wide. 830.5 does not require a call for every incident. It requires immediate notification only for an accident, for the serious incidents it lists, and for an overdue aircraft believed to be in an accident [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

head: Event
Who gets the report
Source
rows: Accident or listed serious incident
NTSB, immediately
Near midair collision (within 500 ft, or a collision hazard reported)
FAA: by radio or phone to the nearest ATC facility or FSS, or in writing to the FSDO
Any safety problem you want to report, without a duty to
NASA, through the voluntary ASRS
Deviation from a rule in an in-flight emergency
FAA, in writing, only if the Administrator asks (taught in RF.VII.A)

callout.text: The AIM says NTSB reporting requirements are separate and distinct from FAA reporting requirements [[34:259|AIM 11-8-4]]. One report never takes the place of the other.

bullets: To make an NMAC report, be specific: say "I wish to report a near midair collision." ATC will not treat a casual remark as a report [[34:178|AIM 7-7-3]].
The FSDO where the NMAC happened investigates it, and if a regulation was broken, enforcement action will be pursued [[34:178|AIM 7-7-3]].

check.q: You pass 300 ft from another airplane with no contact. Do you call the NTSB under 830.5?
check.a: No. A near miss is not on the 830.5 list, which names an aircraft collision in flight [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. It is an NMAC, reported to the FAA through ATC, an FSS or the FSDO [[34:178|AIM 7-7-3]].

chunks.title: The serious incidents that need a call right now

body.p: The operator must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately when an accident or one of these listed serious incidents occurs [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. Nobody has to be hurt.

head: 830.5(a) item
What it says
For a light single (application)
rows: Flight control system malfunction or failure [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Applies. A jammed cable, a disconnected control, a runaway that the system cannot stop
Any required flight crewmember unable to perform normal flight duties because of injury or illness [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Applies. You are the required crewmember
Failure of an internal turbine engine component with debris escaping other than out the exhaust path [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Turbine engines only
In-flight fire [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Applies, even if it goes out and you land with no damage
Aircraft collision in flight [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Applies, even a wingtip touch
Damage to property other than the aircraft, estimated over $25,000 for repair (materials and labor), or fair market value if a total loss, whichever is less [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Applies. Fences, lights, hangars, cars
Four items for large multiengine aircraft over 12,500 lb [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Does not apply
Release of all or part of a propeller blade, except release caused solely by ground contact [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]
Applies
Complete loss of information, excluding flickering, from more than 50 percent of EFIS type cockpit displays, such as a PFD, navigation display and other integrated displays [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]
Applies to glass panels
ACAS resolution advisory on an IFR flight plan when following it is needed to avoid a substantial risk of collision [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]
Only if you have an ACAS that issues resolution advisories
Helicopter rotor blade damage needing major repair or replacement [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]
Helicopters only
Air carrier landing or departing on a taxiway or wrong runway, or a runway incursion needing immediate corrective action [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]
Air carrier operations only

callout.text: Memory aid (our own, not FAA): for a piston single, think "Controls, Crew, Fire, Collision, Property, Prop, Panel, RA." Those are items (1), (2), (4), (5), (6), (8), (9) and (10) [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

body.p: Interpretation of item (9): on a two screen panel, losing one screen is 50 percent, which is not more than 50 percent. Losing both is [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

callout.text: Changed: the AIM list in 7-7-2 stops at the large aircraft items and words the turbine item differently [[34:176|AIM 7-7-2a]] [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]]. 830.5 adds items (8) to (12), and its amendment list ends with 80 FR 77587, Dec. 15, 2015 [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]. Use the CFR list.

check.q: A stone thrown up during taxi nicks a propeller tip. Is this a listed serious incident?
check.a: No. Item (8) excludes blade release caused solely by ground contact, and ground damage to propeller blades is not substantial damage [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

chunks.title: Overdue aircraft, how to notify, and what to say

body.p: 830.5 also requires immediate notice when an aircraft is overdue and is believed to have been involved in an accident [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]. In practice, ARTCCs and FSSs alert the search and rescue system when they learn an aircraft is in difficulty, overdue or missing, and a filed flight plan is the most timely sign that an aircraft is overdue [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f]].

callout.text: The operator must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately and by the most expeditious means available [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. The rule's footnote gives the NTSB Response Operations Center: 844-373-9922 or 202-314-6290 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5 note 1]].

body.p: The AIM says the most expeditious method depends on the circumstances, and gives examples the NTSB accepts: a direct phone call, or notifying the FAA, which then notifies the NTSB [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]].

head: 830.6: give these, if available
Source
rows: Type, nationality and registration marks of the aircraft
Name of the owner and operator
Name of the pilot in command
Date and time of the accident
Last point of departure and point of intended landing
Position, referenced to an easily defined geographical point
Number aboard, number killed, number seriously injured
Nature of the accident, the weather, and the extent of damage, so far as known
Any explosives, radioactive materials or other dangerous articles carried

callout.text: Application: save the Response Operations Center numbers [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5 note 1]] in your phone and on your kneeboard card. You will not want to search for them at the scene.

check.q: Who must make the call, and how fast?
check.a: The operator, immediately, by the most expeditious means available, to the nearest NTSB office [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. The operator is the person who causes or authorizes the operation, such as the owner, lessee or bailee [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

chunks.title: Preserve the wreckage and the records

callout.text: The operator of an aircraft in an accident or incident for which notification must be given must preserve, to the extent possible, the wreckage, cargo and mail aboard, and all records about the operation and maintenance of the aircraft and the airmen, until the Board takes custody or grants a release [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

bullets: Until the Board takes custody, wreckage may not be disturbed or moved except as needed to remove persons injured or trapped, to protect the wreckage from further damage, or to protect the public from injury [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
If wreckage must be moved, make sketches, descriptive notes and photographs, if possible, of the original positions and condition and any significant impact marks [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
Keep all records, reports, internal documents and memoranda about the accident or incident until the Board authorizes otherwise [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

Records include recording media of flight, maintenance and voice recorders [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]]. Operators with approved flight data and cockpit voice recorders installed keep the recorded information at least 60 days after such an event that ends the flight [[60:543|14 CFR 91.609(g)]].

callout.text: Watch out: preservation is not only for accidents. It covers any incident that needs notification [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]]. After an in-flight fire, the burned parts and the maintenance records are evidence; do not let anyone start repairs before the NTSB releases the airplane.

body.p: Before touchdown, the AFH suggests turning off the electrical system and the fuel to reduce the chance of a post-crash fire [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Application: that protects people first and the wreckage second, which is the order 830.10 also uses [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

check.q: Name the three reasons you may move wreckage before the NTSB takes custody.
check.a: To remove persons injured or trapped, to protect the wreckage from further damage, or to protect the public from injury [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

head: Event
Written report
Source
rows: Accident
Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days after the accident
Overdue aircraft
Form 6120.1/2 after 7 days if the aircraft is still missing
Listed serious incident
Only if an authorized representative of the Board asks for it

bullets: Each crewmember who is physically able when the report is submitted must attach a statement of the facts, conditions and circumstances as they appeared to them. An incapacitated crewmember submits it as soon as physically able [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].
File the report with the Board field office nearest the accident or incident [[60:885|49 CFR 830.15(c)]].

Forms are available from Board field offices, Board headquarters in Washington, DC, and FAA Flight Standards District Offices [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15 note 2]]. The FAA has about 80 FSDOs [[1:24|PHAK 1-9]].

callout.text: Note: the AIM calls the form "6120.1 or 6120.2" and lists nine field office cities [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]]. 830.15 names Board Form 6120.1/2 and the nearest field office [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]] [[60:885|49 CFR 830.15(c)]]. Follow the CFR.

check.q: You reported an in-flight fire by phone. Nobody from the NTSB has asked for a written report. Is Form 6120.1/2 due in 10 days?
check.a: No. For a listed incident the report is filed only as requested by an authorized representative of the Board [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

chunks.title: Risk: "Nobody was hurt, so we don't need to report it"

body.p: Injury is only one door into 830. Substantial damage alone makes an accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]], and every listed serious incident needs an immediate call with no injury at all [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

head: What people say
What the rule says
rows: "No one was hurt."
Substantial damage alone is an accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. A fire, flight control failure or collision in flight needs a call regardless [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
"The fire went out, and the airplane is fine."
In-flight fire is on the list. Damage is not a condition [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
"I'll just file an ASRS report."
ASRS is voluntary and goes to NASA [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]]. The FAA may use information about accidents, which are wholly excluded from the program [[60:440|14 CFR 91.25]]
"Let's fix it and forget it."
Wreckage and records must be preserved until the Board takes custody or releases them [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]]
"It was only a near miss."
Not an 830 event, but the FAA wants an NMAC report, made clearly [[34:178|AIM 7-7-3]]

body.p: The AFH warns that a pilot's financial stake in the airplane can bend emergency decisions [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. Application: the same pull, and worry about the certificate, can tempt a pilot to keep quiet afterward. Decide now that you will apply the definitions, not your feelings.

callout.text: ASRS still has a place. Reports to NASA are invited for actual or potential deficiencies, and timely reports (delivered or postmarked within 10 days, on NASA ARC Form 277) earn a waiver of certain disciplinary actions [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]]. File one in addition to, never instead of, the NTSB notice when an incident qualifies.

check.q: Does 91.25 protect the information in your ASRS report about an accident?
check.a: No. 91.25 excludes information about accidents or criminal offenses, which are wholly excluded from the program [[60:440|14 CFR 91.25]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: does this event go to the NTSB?

body.p: **Run the same questions in the same order every time.** Each step comes straight from the 830 definitions and lists [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

bullets: 1. Did it happen between the time someone boarded with the intention of flight and the time all got off? If not, it is not an aircraft accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
2. Did anyone die within 30 days, or meet any of the five serious injury tests? Then it is an accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

3. Is there substantial damage once you set aside the excluded items (engine only, cowling, dents, small holes, ground prop damage, gear, wheels, tires, flaps, accessories, brakes, wingtips)? Then it is an accident [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].
4. If not an accident, is it on the 830.5(a) list, including property damage over $25,000? Then it is a listed serious incident [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].
5. Overdue and believed in an accident? That needs a call too [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].
6. Any yes: the operator calls the nearest NTSB office now, with the 830.6 details [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.6]]. Preserve wreckage and records [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
7. Accident: Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days with each crewmember's statement. Listed incident: only if asked [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].
8. All no: consider an NMAC report to the FAA or an ASRS report to NASA [[34:178|AIM 7-7-3]] [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]].

callout.text: Application: if you are unsure whether damage is substantial or an injury is serious, the cost of calling is a few minutes. The rule asks for immediate notice [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]], and a call lets the NTSB decide what it needs.

check.q: A runaway trim forces you to land holding heavy pressure. No one is hurt and nothing is damaged. Which step answers it?
check.a: Step 4. A flight control system malfunction or failure is a listed serious incident, so the operator notifies the NTSB immediately [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Thinking any damage to the airplane makes an accident
Check the 830.2 list of damage that is not substantial [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]
Thinking no injury means no report
Substantial damage alone is an accident; listed incidents need a call with no injury [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Treating a broken wrist as minor
Any fracture other than simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose is a serious injury [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]
Using the old AIM incident list
Use 830.5, which adds propeller blade release, display loss and ACAS items [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]
Waiting for business hours or for the written report
Notify immediately by the most expeditious means [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]
Letting a mechanic or owner haul the wreckage away
Move it only for the three listed reasons, and photograph it first if possible [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]]
Filing ASRS instead of notifying the NTSB
ASRS does not cover accidents and is separate from 830 [[60:440|14 CFR 91.25]] [[34:259|AIM 11-8-4]]

check.q: Your airplane strikes a runway light during a landing roll. The airport estimates $8,000 to repair the light, and your only damage is a cut tire. Call the NTSB?
check.a: No, by these facts. Property damage must exceed $25,000 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]], and tire damage is not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]. No one was hurt.

scenario.title: Smoke under the panel, and a manager who wants it quiet
scenario.setup: You rent a Cessna 172 from a local flight school for a Saturday trip with a friend. Ten minutes after takeoff, smoke and then small flames appear under the right side of the panel. You turn the master switch off, the flames stop, and you land back at the home field with no injuries. A mechanic finds a burned wiring bundle behind the panel. The school manager says, "Nobody got hurt and it's just wires. We'll fix it Monday, no need for paperwork."

questions.q: Accident, listed serious incident, or neither?
questions.a: Not an accident by these facts: no death or serious injury, and interpretation, burned wiring does not appear to affect structural strength, performance or flight characteristics [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]. But an in-flight fire is a listed serious incident that needs immediate notification [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

questions.q: Who has to notify the NTSB, you or the school?
questions.a: The operator: the person who causes or authorizes the operation, such as the owner, lessee or bailee [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. Interpretation: a rental can make either of you fit that wording, and the rule does not say more. Agree with the school who will call, and make sure the call happens.

questions.q: When and how should the call be made, and what details go in it?
questions.a: Immediately, by the most expeditious means available, to the nearest NTSB office; the Response Operations Center is 844-373-9922 or 202-314-6290 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5 note 1]]. Give the 830.6 items you have, such as the aircraft, owner and operator, PIC, date and time, departure and destination, position, persons aboard and injuries, nature of the event and weather, and any dangerous articles [[60:883|49 CFR 830.6]] [[60:884|49 CFR 830.6]].

questions.q: Can the mechanic replace the wiring on Monday?
questions.a: Not before the NTSB takes custody or releases the airplane. The operator must preserve the wreckage and all records on operation and maintenance for any incident needing notification [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
Only if an authorized NTSB representative asks for it, since this is a listed incident, not an accident. If it is filed, each crewmember who is able attaches a statement [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

questions.q: The manager suggests you file an ASRS report "to cover yourself" instead. What do you say?
questions.a: ASRS is a voluntary NASA program, and timely reports earn a waiver of certain disciplinary actions [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]] [[60:440|14 CFR 91.25]]. It is separate from, and does not replace, the NTSB notice [[34:259|AIM 11-8-4]]. You may file one in addition to the call.

skills.do: Given a short description of an event (who was aboard, injuries, damage, what failed), say whether it is an aircraft accident, a listed serious incident, an overdue aircraft case or none of these, citing the 830.2 definition or 830.5 item. Then say who notifies, how fast, what details to give, what must be preserved, and whether and when Form 6120.1/2 is due.
skills.practice: Make a one-page card with the 830.2 definitions, the excluded damage list and the 830.5(a) items that fit your airplane [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]], plus the Response Operations Center numbers [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5 note 1]]. Then ask a CFI or friend to read you ten short events (or use NTSB final reports like AIH Figure 10-1 [[25:185|AIH 10-1]]) and run the eight steps out loud until each takes under a minute.

quiz.q: Which agency determines the probable cause of a civil aviation accident?
options: The local FSDO
The NTSB
NASA, through ASRS
The aircraft manufacturer
quiz.why: The NTSB determines probable cause and makes recommendations; the FAA looks at its own areas [[30:10|RMH 1-1]].

quiz.q: A passenger hurt in an accident dies 20 days later from those injuries. Under 830.2 this is:
options: A serious injury only, since the death came later
A fatal injury
Not counted, since death was not at the scene
A fatal injury only if the person died in a hospital
quiz.why: A fatal injury is any injury that results in death within 30 days of the accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

quiz.q: Which damage, by itself, is NOT substantial damage under 830.2?
options: Damage that adversely affects structural strength and would normally need major repair
Failure that adversely affects flight characteristics and normally needs replacement of the part
Damage limited to the brakes, one tire and a wingtip
Damage that adversely affects performance and would normally need major repair
quiz.why: Damage to brakes, tires and wingtips is on the excluded list [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

quiz.q: Must every incident, as 830.2 defines it, be reported to the NTSB?
options: Yes, within 10 days
Yes, immediately
No, only the serious incidents listed in 830.5(a) need immediate notification
No, incidents go only to the FAA
quiz.why: An incident is any non-accident occurrence that affects or could affect safety [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]; 830.5 requires immediate notice only for accidents, the listed incidents and certain overdue aircraft [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

quiz.q: Under 830.5(a)(6), damage to property other than the aircraft triggers notification when the estimate exceeds:
quiz.why: Over $25,000 for repair, including materials and labor, or fair market value if a total loss, whichever is less [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

quiz.q: How does 830.5 say the operator must notify the NTSB?
options: In writing within 10 days
Immediately, by the most expeditious means available, to the nearest NTSB office
Through an ASRS report within 10 days
At the next annual inspection
quiz.why: Immediately and by the most expeditious means available, to the nearest NTSB office [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

quiz.q: How long must the operator keep reports, internal documents and memoranda about a reportable accident?
options: 30 days
60 days
Until the insurance claim closes
Until the Board authorizes otherwise
quiz.why: The operator retains them until authorized by the Board to the contrary [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

quiz.q: Where is the written report filed?
options: With the FSDO that issued your certificate
With the Board field office nearest the accident or incident
With NASA in Moffett Field
With the airport manager
quiz.why: File any report with the field office of the Board nearest the accident or incident [[60:885|49 CFR 830.15(c)]].

quiz.q: You file an ASRS report about an accident you had. What does 91.25 say?
options: The FAA can never use it
The FAA may not use it, but the NTSB report is no longer needed
Information about accidents is wholly excluded from the program's protection
ASRS reports replace the 830.15 written report
quiz.why: 91.25 bars FAA enforcement use of ASRS reports except information about accidents or criminal offenses, which are wholly excluded [[60:440|14 CFR 91.25]].

final_quiz.q: After a hard landing, a passenger feels fine. Three days later she is admitted to a hospital and stays 60 hours. Nothing on the airplane is substantially damaged. What applies?
options: Nothing; she was not hurt at the scene
It is an accident: a stay over 48 hours starting within 7 days is a serious injury
It is an incident reported only if the NTSB asks
It becomes an accident only if she stays 7 days
final_quiz.why: Hospitalization for more than 48 hours, starting within 7 days from the injury, is a serious injury [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]], which makes it an accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

final_quiz.q: Taxiing in, your wingtip hits a hangar. The wingtip and its light are broken; the hangar repair estimate is $12,000. Nobody is hurt. What applies?
options: Accident: any collision with a structure
Listed serious incident: property damage
No NTSB notification is required by these facts
Report within 10 days but no call
final_quiz.why: Wingtip damage is not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]], and the property damage is under the $25,000 threshold [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

final_quiz.q: In cruise the PIC has a seizure, and a pilot-rated passenger lands safely. No damage, no other injuries. What applies?
options: Nothing, since the landing was safe
A listed serious incident: a required flight crewmember could not perform normal duties because of illness
An accident, because a seizure is a serious injury
An NMAC report to the FAA
final_quiz.why: Inability of any required flight crewmember to perform normal flight duties because of injury or illness is item (a)(2) [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

final_quiz.q: In cruise a piece of a propeller blade tip separates and the engine shakes. You land with no other damage and no injuries. What applies?
options: Nothing; ground damage to propellers is excluded
A listed serious incident: release of part of a propeller blade not caused solely by ground contact
An accident, since the propeller is substantial damage
Report to the FAA only
final_quiz.why: Release of all or part of a propeller blade, excluding release caused solely by ground contact, is item (a)(8) [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

final_quiz.q: On a VFR flight both screens of your two screen glass panel go completely dark for ten minutes, then come back. What applies?
options: Nothing, since they came back
A listed serious incident: complete loss of information from more than 50 percent of the EFIS displays
Only an ASRS report
An accident
final_quiz.why: Complete loss of information, excluding flickering, from more than 50 percent of EFIS type displays is item (a)(9) [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]. Both of two screens is 100 percent.

final_quiz.q: A friend's airplane is two hours overdue, an alert notice has gone out, and people believe it went down in the mountains. What does 830.5 require?
options: Nothing until wreckage is found
Immediate notification, since an overdue aircraft believed in an accident must be reported
A written report today
Only an FSS search
final_quiz.why: 830.5(b) requires immediate notice when an aircraft is overdue and believed to have been involved in an accident [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]. ARTCCs and FSSs also alert search and rescue [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f]].

final_quiz.q: You rent a club airplane. Under 830, whose duty is it to notify the NTSB of an accident?
options: The control tower that saw it
The operator: the person who causes or authorizes the operation, such as the owner, lessee or bailee
The insurance company
The nearest FSDO
final_quiz.why: 830.5 puts the duty on the operator, defined in 830.2 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

final_quiz.q: Your single has an ACAS that issues resolution advisories. On an IFR flight plan you get one and must follow it to avoid a substantial risk of collision. No contact. What applies?
options: Nothing, since the system worked
A listed serious incident under 830.5(a)(10)
An NMAC report is the only requirement
An accident
final_quiz.why: An ACAS resolution advisory on an IFR flight plan, when compliance is needed to avert a substantial risk of collision, is item (a)(10) [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

final_quiz.q: You reported a listed serious incident by phone. Two weeks later no one at the NTSB has asked for anything. What is overdue?
options: Form 6120.1/2 was due in 10 days
Nothing: a report on a listed incident is filed only as requested
A crewmember statement is due by itself
An ASRS report is required
final_quiz.why: A report on an incident needing immediate notice is filed only as requested by an authorized representative of the Board [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

final_quiz.q: After a reportable accident, the owner's mechanic wants to take the aircraft and engine logbooks home to update them. What does 830.10 say?
options: Fine, logbooks are not part of the wreckage
The operator must preserve all records on the operation and maintenance of the aircraft until the Board takes custody or releases them
Only flight recorder data must be kept
Records may be changed if a copy is kept
final_quiz.why: The operator preserves all records pertaining to operation and maintenance of the aircraft and to the airmen until the Board takes custody or grants a release [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

final_quiz.q: Two airplanes in a formation flight touch wingtips. Both land safely. The only damage is to the wingtips, and no one is hurt. What applies?
options: Nothing: wingtip damage is excluded
A listed serious incident: aircraft collision in flight
An accident because two aircraft were involved
An NMAC report only
final_quiz.why: Wingtip damage is not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]], so it is not an accident, but an aircraft collision in flight is item (a)(5) [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

final_quiz.q: While pushing an empty airplane into a hangar, a line worker bends the wing spar. No one was aboard or planning to fly. Is this an aircraft accident under 830.2?
options: Yes: a bent spar is substantial damage
No, by interpretation: it happened outside the window that starts when someone boards with the intention of flight
Yes, if repair exceeds $25,000
No, because spars are excluded from substantial damage
final_quiz.why: The accident window runs from boarding with the intention of flight until all have disembarked [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Interpretation: with no one aboard for flight, the definition is not met, though the damage itself would be substantial [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about the AIM 7-7-2 list compared with 49 CFR 830.5 is correct?
options: They are identical
The AIM list lacks items such as propeller blade release and cockpit display loss, so use the CFR
The AIM list is newer and replaces the CFR
The CFR list covers only air carriers
final_quiz.why: 830.5 includes items (8) to (12) [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]; AIM 7-7-2 lists only the older items [[34:176|AIM 7-7-2a]] [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]].

takeaways: Accident: someone dies within 30 days or is seriously injured, or the airplane is substantially damaged, between boarding for flight and getting off.
Gear, wheels, tires, brakes, flaps, wingtips, dents, cowling and ground prop damage alone are not substantial damage.
Some incidents need a call with no injury: flight control failure, crew incapacitation, in-flight fire, collision in flight, property over $25,000, propeller blade release, display loss, ACAS RA.
The operator notifies the nearest NTSB office immediately, by the fastest means, with the 830.6 details.
Preserve wreckage and records; move wreckage only to free people, protect it or protect the public, and photograph first if you can.
Form 6120.1/2 is due within 10 days after an accident; for a listed incident only if the NTSB asks.
ASRS and NMAC reports go to NASA and the FAA. They never replace the NTSB notice.
cfi_notes: AIM 7-7-2 is out of step with 49 CFR 830.5: its turbine item reads differently, and it leaves out items (8) to (12), including propeller blade release and display loss [[34:176|AIM 7-7-2a]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]. Teach the CFR list.

AIM 7-7-2 lists nine NTSB field office cities and telegraphic notice, and names Form "6120.1 or 6120.2" [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]]. The CFR footnote gives the Response Operations Center numbers and the form as 6120.1/2 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5 note 1]] [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]]. Use the CFR.

Interpretation: 830 does not define "immediately" or "most expeditious means" [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. The AIM says the circumstances decide [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]]. Teach pilots to call from the scene once people are safe.

The operator definition (owner, lessee, bailee) [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] leaves renters and club members unsure who calls. The sources do not settle it; have pilots agree on it with the school or club in advance.

Whether damage is substantial often needs a mechanic. Link 830.2 "major repair" to the 14 CFR 1.1 definition [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:10|14 CFR 1.1]], and stress that the excluded list is the quick first filter.

AC 61-98E Appendix E does not list 49 CFR 830 [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]], yet 61.105 and 61.125 make it required knowledge [[60:295|14 CFR 61.105(b)(2)]] [[60:310|14 CFR 61.125(b)(2)]]. Add a five-minute 830 drill to flight reviews.
Pilots confuse the 91.3(c) deviation report, NMAC reports, ASRS and 830 notice. Use the chunk 4 table; RF.VII.A covers 91.3 in depth.
Use NTSB final reports such as AIH Figure 10-1 [[25:185|AIH 10-1]] as practice: have the pilot say from the injuries and damage fields why the event was reportable.
The AFH idea of sacrificing the airplane [[24:351|AFH 18-2]] pairs well with this lesson: a pilot who fears the paperwork may make the same bad choices the AFH warns about.
gaps: NTSB Form 6120.1/2 itself, and any online way to file it, are not in the sources.
49 CFR 831 (including the 831.12(b) release that ends the preservation duty) is cited by 830.10 but is not in the sources.
AC 00-46 on the ASRS is named in AIM 7-7-1 but is not in the sources, so the full waiver conditions are not given.
No source says how the FAA treats a pilot after an accident (for example reexamination), or what insurance policies require.
Which specific repairs make damage "substantial" for a given airplane needs a mechanic, the manufacturer's data and the NTSB; the sources give only the definitions.

activities.title: Say it like 830.2
activities.intro: Tap a term, then its meaning.

pairs.r: Death within 30 days of the accident
More than 48 hours, starting within 7 days
Second or third degree, or more than 5 percent of the body
Person who causes or authorizes the operation
Non-accident occurrence that affects or could affect safety
From boarding for flight until all have got off
Hurts strength, performance or handling; needs major repair

activities.title: Dispensable or vital?
activities.intro: Drag each label to the part of the airplane it names.

pins.label: Cabin: the vital structure to keep intact

activities.why: The AFH uses wings, gear and fuselage bottom as dispensable structure to keep the cabin intact [[24:351|AFH 18-2]] [[24:355|AFH 18-6]]. Damage to wheels, tires and wingtips alone is not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

activities.title: Accident, listed incident, or neither?
activities.intro: Each event is in a light single on a Part 91 flight. Tap an event, then where it belongs.
buckets: No NTSB notification by these facts

items.t: Hard landing; a passenger's leg is broken
Runway excursion buckles a wing spar; no one hurt
Aileron cable jams in cruise; safe landing
Overrun damages an airport fence, $30,000 to repair; airplane fine
Smoke and flames from the engine compartment; fire goes out
Engine quits; normal landing in a field, no other damage
Propeller tips bent striking a taxi light, no injuries
Flat tire and a damaged brake after landing

activities.why: Accidents: serious injury or substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]. Interpretation: a buckled spar adversely affects structural strength. Listed incidents: flight control failure, property over $25,000, in-flight fire [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. Engine failure limited to the engine, ground damage to propeller blades, and tire and brake damage are not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

activities.title: Run the numbers in 830
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A passenger is hurt Saturday at 1500. She is admitted to a hospital Monday at 0800 and discharged Wednesday at 1000. How many hours was she hospitalized?
items.why: Monday 0800 to Wednesday 0800 is 48 hours, plus 2 hours = 50. More than 48 hours, starting within 7 days of the injury, so it is a serious injury [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

items.q: Repairing a fence you hit needs $14,800 in materials and $11,600 in labor. By how many dollars does this exceed the 830.5(a)(6) threshold?
A parked car is destroyed. Repair would cost $31,000; its fair market value is $19,500. What dollar figure does 830.5(a)(6) compare with $25,000?
items.why: For a total loss, use repair cost or fair market value, whichever is less: min(31,000, 19,500) = 19,500, which is under $25,000 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

items.q: Your panel has three EFIS displays. What is the smallest number that must lose all information to make it more than 50 percent?
items.why: 1 of 3 = 33 percent; 2 of 3 = 67 percent, which is more than 50 percent [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

items.q: An accident happens on the 5th of the month. The written report is due within 10 days after it. On what date of the same month is the last day?

activities.title: From the crash site to the report
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put these in order, then tap Check.
steps: Get injured or trapped people out, moving wreckage only as needed
Notify the nearest NTSB office immediately by the fastest means
Guard the wreckage until the NTSB takes custody or releases it
File Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days, with each crewmember's statement
Keep the records until the Board says otherwise
activities.why: Moving wreckage to free people [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]]; immediate notice [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] with the 830.6 items [[60:883|49 CFR 830.6]]; preserve until custody or release [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]]; report within 10 days [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]]; retain records [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

activities.title: True or false: after the event
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Each crewmember who is physically able must attach a statement to the written report.
The duty to preserve wreckage and records applies only to accidents, not to incidents.
cards.why: False. It covers any accident or incident for which notification must be given [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

cards.s: NTSB report forms are available from FAA Flight Standards District Offices.
cards.why: True. Also from Board field offices and headquarters [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15 note 2]].

cards.s: ATC will treat a casual remark about a close call as a near midair collision report.
cards.why: False. Say "I wish to report a near midair collision" [[34:178|AIM 7-7-3]].

cards.s: To be timely for the ASRS waiver, a report must be delivered or postmarked within 10 days of the incident, unless extended for good cause.
The AIM says NTSB reporting requirements are separate and distinct from FAA reporting requirements.

activities.title: Off-field landing: what now?
activities.intro: Your Piper Cherokee's engine quits at 2,500 ft AGL. You glide to a plowed field and touch down. The nose gear collapses, the airplane slides to a stop, and you and your passenger climb out. She is holding her wrist, which is swelling and looks crooked.

steps.s: Before thinking about damage: is this already an accident?
options: No, a wrist injury is minor
Yes, if her wrist is fractured: any fracture except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose is a serious injury
Only if she stays in a hospital more than 48 hours
Only if the airplane has substantial damage
steps.why: A fracture of any bone, except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose, is a serious injury [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]], and a serious injury makes it an accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

steps.s: The farmer arrives with a tractor and wants to drag the airplane to his barn so he can plant tomorrow. What do you say?
options: Fine, it is his field
Leave it in place; it may be moved only to free people, protect it from further damage or protect the public, with photos of its original position if moved
Fine, if your insurance agent agrees
Fine, as long as you take one photo afterward
steps.why: Wreckage may not be moved except for those three reasons, and if moved, sketches, notes and photographs of the original positions should be made if possible [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

steps.s: You have no cell coverage, but your handheld radio reaches Flight Service, an FAA facility. What is your best first move?
options: Wait until you get home and call Monday
Report through Flight Service, which the NTSB accepts as a way to notify, then call the NTSB yourself when you have coverage (application)
Send an ASRS report instead
Do nothing until the 10-day written report
steps.why: Notice must be immediate by the most expeditious means [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. The AIM lists notification to the FAA, which then notifies the NTSB, as acceptable [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]].

steps.s: On the phone with the NTSB, which set of facts does 830.6 ask for?
options: Your total flight time, medical class and home address
Aircraft type and registration, owner and operator, PIC, date and time, departure and destination, position, people aboard and injuries, nature, weather and damage, and any dangerous articles
Only the registration number and your name
The cost of repairs and your insurance company
steps.why: Those are the 830.6 items, given if available [[60:883|49 CFR 830.6]] [[60:884|49 CFR 830.6]].

steps.s: Ten days later, what written report is due and where does it go?
options: Nothing unless the NTSB asks
Form 6120.1/2 with your crewmember statement, to the NTSB field office nearest the accident
An ASRS form to NASA only
A letter to the FSDO under 91.3
steps.why: For an accident, the report is due within 10 days with each able crewmember's statement [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]], filed with the field office nearest the accident [[60:885|49 CFR 830.15(c)]].
